title: Post-mortem toxicology: What the dead can and cannot tell us

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and in the one large autopsy registry read here no death was certified as a poisoning by THC, the main active substance of cannabis. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with no stated selection rules or appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that no minimum blood THC level can show cause because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). They relay, second-hand, studies pointing both ways: a heart-attack risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the hour after smoking cannabis in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people, and a higher death rate after a heart attack with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14, in 1,913 people), against no association with death from heart disease in 5,113 young US adults followed for 25 years, and two systematic reviews that disagree; the review's statement that eleven of its twelve tabulated studies showed raised risk is not borne out by its own table (Drummer et al., 2019). In Finland, among 57,903 medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, THC was found in femoral blood in 347 deaths (median 0.002 mg/L, that is 2 ng/mL), and forensic pathologists certified none of them as a fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). THC levels after death are hard to read: THC in femoral blood fell after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026, relayed without sizes), and whole blood, the usual post-mortem sample, has to be multiplied by about 1.6 to compare with the plasma values used for living people (Leikin & Watson, 2003, second-hand). The case reports have no comparison group and cannot show how often THC is present in sudden deaths that cannabis did not cause, so counting cannabis as a cause on the reviewers' criteria would rest on THC being present plus the circumstances. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a risk. Case reports (Drummer et al., 2019): 13 deaths, men aged 17–52 (median 37); coronary disease or other pathology 8/13; blood THC measured in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), urine or history only in 5 (one blood-negative); alcohol in 2 (0.04% and 0.119%). Relayed: acute myocardial infarction 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) within 1 h of smoking, 1.7 (0.6–5.1) within 2 h (case-crossover, n = 3,882); mortality after MI, HR 4.2 (1.2–14) weekly use, 2.5 (0.9–7.3) less than weekly (n = 1,913); CARDIA (n = 5,113, 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality. Finland 2000–2010: THC in femoral blood in 347 deaths, median 0.002 mg/L, 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L, 0% certified as THC poisoning.

claims.statement: A drug concentration measured after death cannot on its own show that the drug caused the death: concentrations in deaths put down to a drug overlap with those in deaths from other causes and with those measured in living patients taking the drug as a treatment, tolerance shifts the level a person can survive, and levels change after death (see the answer on whether levels change after death). In Finland, where police can order a medico-legal investigation of a sudden or unexplained death and the forensic pathologist decides whether to test for drugs (over 13% of all deaths), one laboratory measured femoral-blood levels in 57,903 deaths of all causes with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, sampled on average five days after death; for 46 of 129 drugs the median level was above the range measured in living patients' plasma during treatment, by up to 100-fold, for 61 it was within that range and for 22 below it. The median for methadone (207 deaths) and for buprenorphine (671 deaths) lay within the treatment range although forensic pathologists certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings by that drug, and the authors state that for strong opioids the level after death plays a limited part in judging the cause, because of tolerance; the medians mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out levels too low to measure, and compare whole blood with plasma ranges (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). In 77 deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England (1992 to 2008), femoral-blood MDMA overlapped widely between deaths put down to MDMA (0.478 to 53.9 mg/L in 13 with a value) and deaths from injuries (0.035 to 4.81 mg/L in 24), although the median was about 7 times higher in the first group (editors' calculation; Milroy, 2011; see the answer on MDMA levels). A 1977 Michigan series, as a 1996 narrative review describes it, found blood morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes, such as injuries or homicide, in 74% of deaths put down to heroin overdose (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand; see the answer on heroin 'overdoses'). A clinical pharmacologist's review adds, second-hand, that published 'lethal' ranges are wide and overlap (for example 40 to 8,500 µg/L quoted for MDMA and 60 to 3,100 µg/L for methadone), that amounts that would kill a person without tolerance are survived by people who use heroin regularly, and that a fatal level could only be defined by classing deaths as caused by the drug or not without knowing the measured levels and then comparing the two groups (Ferner, 2008), which none of the studies read here did; a 2003 practitioners' review lists nine questions a toxicologist should answer before judging a drug's role, among them where the blood was taken, whether the drug changes after death, what is known of the person's tolerance and whether the autopsy findings fit (Leikin & Watson, 2003). Both directions follow: a level that looks high can lead to a death being put down to a drug that was only present, and an ordinary or low level does not rule a drug out. At one North Carolina centre that kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths (2016 to 2021), 265 of 2,719 deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug deaths (9.75%) were given a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology, some with drugs present and some with none found (the split is not reported), while 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were judged drug deaths; the pathologists counted any illicit drug found as at least contributing unless a catastrophic other cause was found (Hancock et al., 2024; see the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing). In these studies the people who decided the cause of death knew the measured levels, and none compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Finland 2000–2010 (57,903 deaths; 129 drugs): median femoral concentration above the therapeutic plasma range for 46 drugs (35.7%), within for 61 (47%), below for 22 (17%); with the stated rule applied consistently, about 48, 58 and 23 (editors' calculation on the card); largest ratio to the upper therapeutic limit 100 (hydroxychloroquine). Methadone median 0.40 mg/L (therapeutic 0.1–0.5), 43% certified poisonings; buprenorphine 0.0012 mg/L (0.0005–0.005), 45%; morphine 0.07 mg/L (0.01–0.1), 4%. Sheffield 1992–2008: MDMA deaths 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49; n = 13), injury deaths 0.035–4.81 mg/L (median 0.483; n = 24); at least 7 of the 13 inside the injury range (editors' calculation). Michigan 1977 (second-hand): 74% of heroin overdose deaths with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes. Quoted lethal ranges (second-hand): MDMA 40–8,500 µg/L, methadone 60–3,100 µg/L. North Carolina 2016–2021: 265/2,719 (9.75%) suspected drug deaths with a non-drug final cause; 115/237 (48.5%, editors' calculation) of deaths not suspected judged drug deaths. No intervals.

claims.statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that cannot be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about 1 to 2 hours before death, every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences to drug diffusing out of organs after death, but no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) found, where the same case had both values, median ratios to femoral blood across drugs of 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with tenfold or larger differences between drugs for most specimens (for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no range or interval is given for any ratio, and cause of death and time since death could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 studies selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that the first sample in these human studies was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so earlier change was not seen. It gives no sizes, does not appraise the studies, judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio shows that change after death occurred but not how much, and concludes that the size of the change cannot yet be tied to drug properties or to features of the case (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists single approximate heart-to-peripheral blood ratios for about 100 drugs without case numbers or sources (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3), higher than the compilation's paired medians for several of the same drugs (Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or lower, for drugs that break down or are lost after death. The evidence consists of selected case series, an unappraised compilation dominated by published poisoning cases, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses): highest to lowest blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold per drug (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Paired median ratios to femoral blood across drugs (number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h); rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Single heart-to-peripheral ratios without case numbers (narrative review): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3. No intervals anywhere.

claims.statement: Deaths recorded as heroin 'overdoses' often involve other drugs, delays and other mechanisms, so the label does not show that heroin alone caused the death, but which substance or mechanism was decisive in a given death cannot be read from the toxicology. In a 1996 narrative review of medical examiners' and coroners' series and official statistics, mostly from 1967 to 1996 in the USA, Australia and Europe, chosen by the authors without a stated search and leaning on their own New South Wales series of 152 heroin-related deaths in 1992, morphine (the substance heroin becomes in the body) was the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% to 48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose across six studies; alcohol was detected in 29% to 75% across 13 studies, with mean blood alcohol of 0.09 to 0.16 g/100 mL where reported, and benzodiazepines in 12% to 55% across four; which drugs each laboratory looked for, and how each source defined a heroin death, is not given (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand). Blood morphine was lower in deaths with alcohol in the five studies that compared them, with weak correlations where reported (r = −0.14 in 505 deaths; r = −0.28 in the authors' series); a third of the authors' series had morphine below the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L); and a 1977 Michigan series found 74% with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes (Darke & Zador, 1996). Many deaths were not instant: 14% of the authors' series were classed as instant and 22% took more than 3 hours, other series found intervals of more than 2 or 3 hours in 44% and 52%, and other people were present at more than half of the deaths in four studies (58% to 79% where a figure was given; Darke & Zador, 1996). The reviewers write that 'overdose' 'may correctly apply to only a minority of heroin-related deaths' and propose 'multiple drug toxicity' for many of them; but finding other drugs does not show that they caused the death, the comparison with survivors rests on three studies cited without figures, tolerance was measured in no study, and low morphine can also reflect a death hours after the last injection, when morphine had already fallen, or change after death (Darke & Zador, 1996). In England and Wales in 2000, of 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths that coroners reported to a national register (the National Programme of Substance Abuse Deaths; reporting voluntary, coverage not stated), the register's researchers classed 802 (77%) as direct overdoses and 235 (23%) as other mechanisms: choking on stomach contents and other acute events (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18). Heroin or morphine was named as implicated in 424 of the direct overdoses and found after death in 488, and was implicated in 42 of the 74 acute events, 33 of the 72 deaths with a drug-related medical condition and 11 of the 18 infections; alcohol was found after death in 316 (39.4%) of the direct overdoses; methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses but was the only drug implicated in 4%. These figures are the researchers' reading of coroners' returns that recorded only drugs found, not a check of official statistics, which were not compared (Webb et al., 2003). In the other direction, heroin can be missed: 6-MAM, the marker that shows heroin rather than another source of morphine, fell in femoral blood after death in bodies sampled more than once (Borra et al., 2026), and a review table reports, second-hand, that testing the fluid around the brain and spinal cord for 6-MAM detected 46% more heroin-related deaths than testing blood (Leikin & Watson, 2003). The evidence is old (before fentanyl), largely second-hand, and from series chosen by the authors or from a register. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Morphine the only drug detected: 23%–48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose (six studies); alcohol detected 29%–75% (13 studies), mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL; benzodiazepines 12%–55% (four studies). Morphine lower with alcohol: r = −0.14 (505 deaths), −0.28. A third below 0.16 mg/L (one series); 74% no higher than people who used heroin and died of other causes (one 1977 series). Instant deaths 14% and over 3 h 22% (one series); over 2 h 44%, over 3 h 52% (two series); others present 58%–79%. All second-hand, no intervals. England and Wales 2000 (1,037 accidental deaths): direct overdose 802 (77%); other mechanisms 235 (23%); heroin/morphine implicated in 424 and found in 488 direct overdoses; implicated in 42/74 acute events, 33/72 drug-related medical conditions, 11/18 infections; alcohol found in 316 (39.4%) direct overdoses; methadone implicated in 13% of direct overdoses, the only drug implicated in 4%. 6-MAM in cerebrospinal fluid: 46% more heroin-related deaths detected than in blood (second-hand).
